Waist-to-height ratio explained

Your waist measurement divided by your height is a simple screening idea that goes beyond BMI. This guide covers how to measure, what the numbers mean, and the limits.

Educational estimates only. Results are not medical advice, a diagnosis, or a treatment plan. Talk to a qualified healthcare professional about your health. Read the full medical disclaimer.

Why use it at all?

BMI cannot show where fat sits on the body. Fat around the abdomen is linked to increased health risk, which is why NICE recommends adults with a BMI under 35 also use waist-to-height ratio as a practical estimate of central fat.

How to measure your waist

NICE advises finding the bottom of your ribs and the top of your hips, wrapping a tape measure around your waist halfway between them (usually just above the belly button), and measuring after breathing out naturally. Measure your height too, and use the same units for both, for example both in centimetres or both in inches.

Working it out

Divide waist by height. NICE gives this example: 96.5 cm divided by 170 cm is 0.57. Or let the waist-to-height ratio calculator do the conversion for you.

What the bands mean

NICE describes a ratio of 0.40 to 0.49 as healthy central fat, 0.50 to 0.59 as increased, and 0.60 or more as high. Its simple message is to try to keep your waist to less than half your height. These are screening bands, not a diagnosis.

Limits

The NHS notes its calculator is not suitable for people with a growth disorder or a BMI over 35, and it is intended for adults. Measurement error matters too: a few centimetres of difference in where the tape sits can change the result, so measure the same way each time. Pair it with the BMI calculator and, if you want to follow changes, the measurement tracker. If your ratio concerns you, speak to a healthcare professional.

Sources and further reading

  • NICE guideline NG246: Identifying and assessing overweight, obesity and central adiposity
